Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel isolated and set apart from others
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: At 35, Vikram Patel functions as a tax consultant in a downtown Chicago high-rise, yet his professional routine has been quietly dismantled by the trauma he endured years ago as a relief worker in a war zone. The turning point arrived when a mortar strike collapsed a makeshift clinic during a supply run. As the structure imploded, the acrid plume of burning insulation instantly hijacked his attention, dragging a fragmented, confusing sequence of collapsing walls and trapped patients into his awareness before he could process the disaster. That visceral intrusion of the past quickly cemented a devastating conviction: the world had grown utterly treacherous, his core beliefs about safety and order completely shattered, and he had fundamentally failed to protect those who depended on him. Now, back in civilian life, the olfactory echo of a fire drill at his firm acts as a potent catalyst. When the smell of smoke wafts through the ventilation system, his nervous system floods with hypervigilance, and his concentration splinters as he frantically scans the open-plan floor for exits. This physiological alarm doesn’t stay confined to his body; it bleeds into his perception, making ordinary client disputes feel like life-threatening confrontations, which in turn causes him to catastrophize any sudden expression of anger from his colleagues. When a senior partner raises his voice during a quarterly review, the perceived threat of social aggression immediately replays the clinic’s chaos in his mind, reinforcing the belief that his presence is inherently dangerous and that he must separate himself from everyone to prevent further harm. To manage this escalating dread, he habitually avoids the conference rooms where high-stakes negotiations occur, and when cornered by aggressive deadlines, he instinctively covers his face with his hands to block the perceived aggression. This deliberate withdrawal starves his brain of corrective evidence; by stepping away, he inadvertently reinforces the distorted appraisal that he is fundamentally compromised, which then amplifies his baseline threat sensitivity and makes him hypersensitive to ordinary auditory cues. The constant scanning for danger, particularly at night when the house is quiet, leaves him perpetually on edge, causing him to jump at routine creaks in the plumbing or distant traffic, a startle response that further fragments his memory consolidation and forces him to confront the bodily reenactment of crouching behind debris. Because he refuses to sit through happy gatherings or hopeful planning sessions, fearing that joy would be a cruel betrayal of his guilt, and deliberately avoids funerals or cemeteries where grief feels inescapable, he isolates himself in a sterile routine. This avoidance ensures that unprocessed trauma memories remain raw and unanchored, continuously feeding back into his negative appraisals of personal failure and world unpredictability, which then lowers his threshold for triggering again. The more he flees positive engagement, the more his threat system overfires at minor stimuli, locking the cycle in place and leaving his body braced for disaster. It was this tightening knot of exhaustion, the way a simple handshake now sends him flinching, and the realization that he could no longer navigate his own firm or support his wife that finally drove him to seek help, though he remains terrified that stepping into therapy means facing the very shame and powerlessness he has spent years trying to outrun.
